result.title: Power Structures in Space: How Sci-Fi Predicts Real-World Politics
result.subject_line: The Senate on the Orbital Station Is Your Senate
result.content_text:
_Why the best political science fiction isn't fiction at all._

Last month, the FCC quietly opened a comment period on satellite constellation governance. A handful of policy wonks noticed. Almost no one else did. Meanwhile, millions of people are reading about the Outer Planets Alliance fighting Belt extraction quotas in The Expanse, or watching a galactic senate collapse under the weight of its own procedural rot in Foundation. The gap between those two facts is exactly what this newsletter exists to close. Science fiction doesn't predict the future in any mystical sense. It runs simulations. It builds a pressure chamber, cranks up the heat, and shows you what breaks first. Right now, the chamber is running hot, and the fiction is keeping pace.

## Worldbuilding as Ideology

Every fictional universe encodes a political argument. Dune's feudal interstellar houses aren't exotic invention, they're a direct critique of how resource monopolies (spice, oil, water) concentrate power in hereditary hands while everyone downstream negotiates scraps. Herbert wasn't writing about Arrakis. He was writing about the Persian Gulf.

The term 'worldbuilding as ideology' has become standard in political-scifi criticism for good reason. [The best analysts in the field](https://fivebooks.com/best-books/the-best-political-science-fiction-arkady-martine/) treat a fictional constitution, trade route, or caste system the way a political scientist treats a real one: as a set of choices that reveal assumptions about who deserves power and who doesn't.

When Asimov's Foundation posits that a single mathematical discipline can predict civilizational collapse, that's not optimism about science. It's a claim about technocracy, that the right experts, given enough data, should govern. Read it in 2025 and you'll hear echoes of every 'evidence-based policy' debate you've sat through.

## The Belt Is Everywhere: Core, Periphery, and Extraction

The Expanse is the most politically literate space opera written in the last twenty years, and its central tension isn't aliens or war. It's labor and resource extraction. The Belt, asteroid miners supplying Earth and Mars with raw materials while living in recycled air and rationed water, maps almost perfectly onto colonial periphery theory. The core extracts. The margin dies slowly and calls it a living.

This isn't coincidence. Contemporary political-scifi criticism consistently uses the core-periphery framework to analyze space settings, treating resource-rich moons and asteroid belts the way historians treat colonial frontiers. [Scholarship on the Cold War 'view from outer space'](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/social-science-history/article/view-from-outer-space-science-fiction-and-political-fantasy-in-the-cold-war-united-states/A37708AE984C124A95C2C84293F2E7AC) argues that imagining power from orbit has always been bound up with real geopolitical fantasy, who controls the high ground controls everything below it.

Today's debates about satellite constellations, lunar resource rights, and deep-sea mining follow the same grammar. The fiction just names it more honestly.

## Corporate Sovereignty and the Privatized Frontier

There's a recurring scene in political science fiction: a corporate representative sits across from a government official, and it becomes clear, slowly, that the corporation has more ships, more data, and more lawyers. The government official knows it too.

The trope of megacorporations owning stations, ships, or resource rights is one of the most-analyzed motifs in contemporary sci-fi criticism, and for obvious reasons. SpaceX holds launch contracts that no government agency can currently match. Starlink's satellite network became a geopolitical instrument in Ukraine before anyone wrote the regulatory framework to govern it. The fiction wasn't early. It was on time.

Le Guin was more subtle about it. The Left Hand of Darkness isn't a corporate story, but its Ekumen, a loose network of worlds that trades in information rather than force, asks the same question every trade bloc asks: what does membership cost, and who sets the terms? Sovereignty, in her telling, is always negotiated. It is never simply held.

The readers who complain that [new sci-fi is 'too political'](https://www.reddit.com/r/scifi/comments/10vzybt/the_amount_of_politics_in_the_newest_science/) are reacting to explicitness, not novelty. The politics were always there. Authors are just done being polite about it.

## AI Governance and the Technocracy Problem

Asimov's psychohistory is an algorithm. So is the AI administrator running a city-ship in Becky Chambers' work, or the predictive systems managing planetary economies in a dozen recent releases. The question these stories keep asking is simple and unanswerable: if a machine makes better decisions than a council, does the council still matter?

This is not a hypothetical. Algorithmic systems already allocate social housing in some cities, set bail recommendations in US courts, and flag content for removal across platforms used by billions. The accountability question, who do you argue with when the system is wrong, is identical in fiction and in practice.

Military SF tends to answer the question one way: technocracy works if the right people control the machine. Solarpunk and hopepunk answer it another way: the machine should be governed by the community it serves, or it shouldn't exist. These aren't aesthetic differences. They're competing theories of legitimacy, dressed in spacesuits.

## What the Fiction Gets Wrong, and Why That Matters

Political science fiction is a thought experiment, not a forecast. The phrasing 'predicts real-world politics' is useful shorthand, but it flattens something important. Fiction compresses. It gives factions clean motives and crises clean edges. Real power structures are slower, murkier, and more boring in their mechanisms.

Bureaucracy, for instance, is one of the most effective political weapons ever invented, and fiction almost always underplays it. Orwell understood this. The Ministry of Truth isn't terrifying because it's violent. It's terrifying because it's tedious, procedural, and staffed by people who go home for dinner. The form you can't file. The committee that never meets. The regulation written to be unreadable. These are the instruments that actually consolidate power, and they're hard to dramatize.

The best political sci-fi acknowledges this gap. [Arkady Martine's recommended reading list](https://fivebooks.com/best-books/the-best-political-science-fiction-arkady-martine/) consistently points toward books where institutional inertia and bureaucratic capture do more damage than any villain. That's the simulation worth running. Not 'what if the emperor is evil?' but 'what if the system works exactly as designed, and the design is the problem?'

Upcoming releases in 2026, tracked through [publisher announcements](https://lithub.com/26-sci-fi-and-fantasy-books-to-look-forward-to-in-2026/) and [anticipated titles lists](https://everybookadoorway.com/unmissable-fantasy-and-scifi-of-2026/), continue to foreground colonization, resistance, and institutional collapse as central themes. The market for this kind of fiction is not shrinking. Neither are the conditions that produce it.

The simulation is only useful if you run it honestly. That means reading the fiction that makes you uncomfortable, not just the fiction that confirms your politics. It means noticing when a space empire you're rooting for is extracting resources from a periphery you've stopped thinking about. It means asking, every time a council votes or a corporation signs a contract in a novel, who wrote the rules that made that moment possible.

So here's the question for this week: which piece of political science fiction changed how you read a real-world institution, a trade agreement, a regulatory body, an election system? Drop your answer in the comments, or reply directly. The best responses will anchor the next issue, which takes on planetary sovereignty and the fiction of consent in federal systems. See you in two weeks.
